text:
# 什么是 AI 机器人屏蔽（AI Bot Blocking）？

- 原标题：What Is AI Bot Blocking?
- 作者：Flavio Amiel Roborank 创始人
- 原文更新日期：2026-07-15
- 原文：https://roborank.io/glossary/ai-bot-blocking/
- 栏目：[AI Search & GEO](https://roborank.io/ai-search/)
- 说明：中文全文翻译，后附英文原文。原文中的数据、观点、平台说明及推广内容均按原文保留，未经独立验证。

---

## 中文全文

AI 机器人屏蔽，是利用 robots.txt 指令，有时再配合服务器级规则，阻止 AI 爬虫获取网站页面的做法。它通过 User-Agent 标识按爬虫分别应用，让运营者根据目标是阻止模型训练、搜索索引，还是两者兼有，选择拒绝某些 AI 机器人，同时允许另一些。

### 核心要点

- 在 robots.txt 中，逐个写出 User-Agent 标识，例如 `User-agent: GPTBot`、`User-agent: CCBot` 等，再跟上 `Disallow: /`，即可屏蔽相应 AI 机器人；没有一条指令可以统一涵盖所有 AI 机器人。
- 屏蔽针对用途，而非公司：OpenAI 的 GPTBot 用于训练，OAI-SearchBot 用于 ChatGPT 搜索，它们遵循不同标识，因此可以拒绝一个、允许另一个。
- 核心取舍是训练使用与 AI 搜索可见性：屏蔽搜索爬虫可以保护内容，但也会让你退出越来越多出现在自然结果上方的 AI 答案。
- 一项 2026 年 4 月针对美国和英国排名前 100 家新闻网站的研究发现，79% 至少屏蔽一个 AI 训练机器人，但只有 14% 屏蔽了研究检查的全部 AI 机器人。

### AI 机器人屏蔽如何运作

AI 机器人屏蔽从域名根目录下的一份纯文本文件开始：robots.txt。遵守规范的 [AI 爬虫](https://roborank.io/glossary/ai-crawler/)会在抓取页面前读取该文件，并遵守针对自身 User-Agent 标识的规则。要屏蔽一个爬虫，就写出它的标识并禁止访问。例如 OpenAI 的训练爬虫，一行写 `User-agent: GPTBot`，下一行写 `Disallow: /`。没有一条指令表示“所有 AI 机器人”，所以想阻止哪个爬虫，就必须分别写出它的名称。

这很重要，因为这些标识对应的是用途，不只是公司。仅 OpenAI 就运行三个：用于模型训练的 [GPTBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/gptbot/)、用于 ChatGPT 搜索索引的 [OAI-SearchBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/oai-searchbot/)，以及用于用户触发访问的 ChatGPT-User。再加上用于 Common Crawl 公开数据集的 [CCBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/ccbot/)、Anthropic 的 ClaudeBot、用于 Gemini 训练的 [Google-Extended](https://roborank.io/glossary/google-extended/)，以及 [PerplexityBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/perplexitybot/)，就形成了十多个独立开关，每个控制你的内容的一种不同用途。

robots.txt 依靠自愿遵守，这是它的局限。行为规范的爬虫会尊重它，但抓取程序可以忽略文件，也可以伪装成受信任的 User-Agent。当自愿遵守不足以满足要求，运营者就会升级到服务器级屏蔽：将连接 IP 与爬虫公布的地址范围列表匹配，OpenAI、Common Crawl 和 Google 都会公布各自的列表，再拒绝无法通过验证的请求。另一种更清晰、面向未来的意图表达方式，是 [llms.txt](https://roborank.io/glossary/llms-txt/)，一种用于声明 AI 系统如何使用网站的提议文件。

### 取舍：训练使用与 AI 搜索可见性

每个屏蔽决定都面临一组张力。屏蔽训练爬虫，可以让自己的文字不进入下一代模型，而不损失搜索表现；屏蔽*搜索*爬虫，则在保护内容的同时，也会让自己从 ChatGPT 搜索结果、Google AI Overviews 等越来越多位于自然链接上方的 AI 答案中消失。两个目标方向相反，而标识的拆分让你可以同时采取两种立场：拒绝 GPTBot 的训练用途，但仍允许 OAI-SearchBot 引用你。直接使用一刀切的 `Disallow: /`，会抹去这种区别，并悄悄损失你原本可能想保留的 [AI 可见性](https://roborank.io/glossary/ai-visibility/)。

### AI 机器人屏蔽示例

BuzzStream 于 2026 年 4 月发布的一项分析，具体测量了按 SimilarWeb 流量排名的美国和英国前 100 家新闻网站，如何在 robots.txt 中处理这个问题。研究检查了 11 个 AI 相关爬虫的禁止访问规则。最醒目的结果是：**79% 至少屏蔽一个 AI 训练机器人**。这说明，对于大型出版商，拒绝 AI 抓取如今已是常态，而非例外。

逐个机器人查看，才能看出取舍。CCBot 的被屏蔽比例最高，为 **75%**；其次是 Anthropic 的旧标识 anthropic-ai，为 72%，以及 ClaudeBot，为 69%；GPTBot 为 **62%**，Google-Extended 则是最少被屏蔽的训练标识，为 **46%**。一个可能的原因，是出版商担心对 Google 产生附带影响。关键在于，选择并非非此即彼：**71%** 至少屏蔽一个实时搜索或检索机器人，但只有 **14%** 屏蔽了研究检查的全部 AI 机器人，另有 **18%** 一个也没屏蔽。

这种分布才说明了真实情况。如果屏蔽 AI 机器人只是一个总开关，网站应该集中在“全部屏蔽”和“全部允许”两个极端。但实际上，大多数处于中间：屏蔽自己不接受的训练爬虫，同时开放足够多的搜索爬虫，以保留被引用的机会。这正是这种做法原本应有的用途：不是一道墙，而是一组独立的门，每扇门都有各自开启或关闭的理由。

### 人们常犯的错误

我看到团队经常犯的错误是，只因为读到一条关于 AI 抓取的惊悚新闻，就立刻使用 `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /`。这个通配规则说的不是“不允许 AI”，而是“不允许任何人”；实际执行中，它会悄悄把决定 ChatGPT 和 Google AI 答案能否引用你的搜索爬虫也赶走。屏蔽不是一个决定，而是针对每个机器人的独立决定。更成熟的做法，是分开回答两个问题：我介不介意内容用于训练模型？我介不介意自己在 AI 搜索里不可见？然后逐个标识作出独立选择。大多数人原本只是想回答第一个问题。

### 常见问题

#### 怎样在 robots.txt 中屏蔽 AI 机器人？

列出每个爬虫的 User-Agent 标识并禁止访问，例如先写 `User-agent: GPTBot`，再写 `Disallow: /`；对 CCBot、ClaudeBot、Google-Extended 等重复这一做法。不存在只针对 AI 机器人的通配符，因此要阻止遵守规范的爬虫，必须逐个点名。

#### 屏蔽 AI 爬虫会损害 SEO 吗？

它不会影响使用 Googlebot 的传统 Google 排名，但可能损害 AI 搜索可见性。屏蔽 OAI-SearchBot 或 Google-Extended 等搜索爬虫，会让你退出 ChatGPT 和 AI Overview 的引用，因此风险在于失去 AI 答案中的出现机会，而不是传统蓝色链接排名。

#### AI 机器人真的遵守 robots.txt 吗？

主要且有文档说明的爬虫——GPTBot、OAI-SearchBot、CCBot、ClaudeBot、Google-Extended——都表示会尊重 robots.txt。但该文件依靠自愿遵守，不良抓取者可以忽略规则或伪装 User-Agent。若要强制执行，需要根据经过核实的 IP 范围，在服务器层面屏蔽。

#### 我到底该不该屏蔽 AI 机器人？

这取决于目标。如果反对内容用于模型训练，就屏蔽训练爬虫；如果希望在 AI 答案里获得引用，就允许搜索爬虫。由于标识彼此独立，大多数网站不必在全部允许和全部拒绝之间二选一，可以选择性屏蔽。

### 要点总结

AI 机器人屏蔽是针对各个爬虫的控制，不是一个总开关：你在 robots.txt 中写出每个 User-Agent 标识，逐个决定是否拒绝。背后的真正问题是一种取舍：一边是不让内容进入模型训练，另一边是保持在 AI 生成答案中的可见性；标识的拆分，让你能够同时采取这两种立场。

## 英文原文

AI bot blocking is the practice of using robots.txt directives, and sometimes server-level rules, to stop AI crawlers from fetching a site’s pages. It is applied per crawler by user-agent token, letting an operator refuse some AI bots while allowing others, depending on whether the goal is to block model training, search indexing, or both.

### Key Takeaways

- AI bots are blocked in robots.txt by naming each user-agent token — `User-agent: GPTBot`, `User-agent: CCBot`, and so on — followed by `Disallow: /`; there is no single directive that covers them all.
- Blocking is per purpose, not per company: OpenAI’s GPTBot (training) and OAI-SearchBot (ChatGPT search) obey different tokens, so you can block one and allow the other.
- The core tradeoff is training exposure versus AI-search visibility — blocking search crawlers protects content but removes you from AI answers that increasingly sit above organic results.
- An April 2026 study of the top 100 US and UK news sites found 79% block at least one AI training bot, but only 14% block every AI bot examined.

### How AI Bot Blocking Works

AI bot blocking starts in one plain text file: robots.txt, at the root of your domain. A compliant [AI crawler](https://roborank.io/glossary/ai-crawler/) reads that file before fetching pages and obeys any rule addressed to its user-agent token. To block one, you write its token and disallow it — for OpenAI’s training crawler, `User-agent: GPTBot` on one line and `Disallow: /` on the next. There is no directive that means “all AI bots,” so each crawler you want to stop has to be named on its own.

The reason this matters is that the tokens map to purposes, not just companies. OpenAI alone runs three: [GPTBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/gptbot/) for model training, [OAI-SearchBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/oai-searchbot/) for ChatGPT search indexing, and ChatGPT-User for user-triggered fetches. Add [CCBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/ccbot/) for Common Crawl’s public dataset, ClaudeBot for Anthropic, [Google-Extended](https://roborank.io/glossary/google-extended/) for Gemini training, and [PerplexityBot](https://roborank.io/glossary/perplexitybot/), and the picture is a dozen independent switches, each governing a different use of your content.

Robots.txt is voluntary, which is its limitation. Well-behaved crawlers honor it, but a scraper can ignore the file or spoof a trusted user-agent string. When compliance is not enough, operators escalate to server-level blocking — matching the connecting IP against a crawler’s published range list (OpenAI, Common Crawl, and Google all publish theirs) and refusing requests that do not verify. A cleaner, forward-looking option for stating intent is [llms.txt](https://roborank.io/glossary/llms-txt/), a proposed file for declaring how AI systems may use a site.

### The tradeoff: training exposure vs AI-search visibility

Every blocking decision sits on a tension. Block a training crawler and you keep your words out of the next model, but you give up nothing in search. Block a *search* crawler and you protect content while also disappearing from the AI answers — ChatGPT search results, Google’s AI Overviews — that increasingly sit above the organic links. The two goals pull in opposite directions, and the token split is what lets you hold both positions: refuse GPTBot’s training use while still allowing OAI-SearchBot to cite you. Reaching for a blanket `Disallow: /` collapses that nuance and quietly costs you the [AI visibility](https://roborank.io/glossary/ai-visibility/) you may have wanted to keep.

### Example of AI Bot Blocking

A BuzzStream analysis published in April 2026 measured exactly how the top 100 news sites in the US and UK — ranked by SimilarWeb traffic — handle this in their robots.txt, checking disallow rules across 11 AI-related crawlers. The headline: **79% block at least one AI training bot**, confirming that among major publishers, refusing AI scraping is now the norm rather than the exception.

The per-bot breakdown is where the tradeoff shows up. CCBot was the most-blocked at **75%**, followed by Anthropic’s legacy anthropic-ai at 72% and ClaudeBot at 69%; GPTBot sat at **62%** and Google-Extended was the least-blocked training bot at **46%** — plausibly because publishers are wary of any collateral effect on Google. Crucially, the choices were not all-or-nothing: **71%** block at least one live search or retrieval bot, yet only **14%** block every AI bot examined, and **18%** block none at all.

The distribution tells the real story. If AI bot blocking were a single on/off decision, you would expect sites clustered at “block all” or “block none.” Instead most land in the middle — blocking the training crawlers they object to while keeping enough search crawlers open to stay citable. That is the practice working as designed: not a wall, but a set of individual doors, each opened or closed on its own reasoning.

### The thing people get wrong

The mistake I watch teams make is reaching for `User-agent: *` / `Disallow: /` because they read one alarming headline about AI scraping. That wildcard does not say "no AI" — it says "no anyone," and in practice it quietly evicts the search crawlers that decide whether ChatGPT and Google’s AI answers can cite you at all. Blocking is not one decision; it is a decision per bot. The sophisticated move is to separate the two questions — do I mind my content training a model, and do I mind being invisible in AI search? — and answer them independently, token by token. Most people only meant to answer the first one.

### Frequently Asked Questions

#### How do I block AI bots in robots.txt?

List each crawler’s user-agent token and disallow it, for example `User-agent: GPTBot` then `Disallow: /`, repeated for CCBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended, and others. There is no wildcard that targets only AI bots, so compliant crawlers must be named individually to be blocked.

#### Does blocking AI crawlers hurt my SEO?

It does not affect classic Google rankings, which use Googlebot, but it can hurt AI-search visibility. Blocking search crawlers like OAI-SearchBot or Google-Extended removes you from ChatGPT and AI Overview citations, so the risk is lost presence in AI answers, not lost blue-link rankings.

#### Do AI bots actually obey robots.txt?

Major documented crawlers — GPTBot, OAI-SearchBot, CCBot, ClaudeBot, Google-Extended — state that they respect robots.txt. But the file is voluntary, so bad actors can ignore it or spoof user agents. For enforcement you need server-level blocking by verified IP range.

#### Should I block AI bots or not?

It depends on your goal. Block training crawlers if you object to your content feeding models; keep search crawlers allowed if you want citations in AI answers. Because the tokens are separate, most sites do not need an all-or-nothing choice and can block selectively.

### The Bottom Line

AI bot blocking is a per-crawler control, not a switch: you name each user-agent token in robots.txt and decide, bot by bot, whether to refuse it. The real question underneath is a tradeoff — keeping content out of model training on one side, staying visible in AI-generated answers on the other — and the token split is what lets you take both positions at once.
